# Programming Activity
<!-- Slide 44 -->

## Part 1: Build It

1. Write a base class with one `virtual` member function that prints a line, and two child classes that inherit publicly and override it. Use your own idea, or Instrument, Guitar, and Drum.
2. In `main`, create one object of each class.
3. Build an array of pointers to the base class that points at all three objects.
4. Loop over the array and call the function through each pointer.

::: notes
Slides 45–49

About 10 minutes. The goal of Part 1 is to see what a working polymorphic array looks like before breaking it. Students who are stuck can model it on Topic 4's Dogs and Cats, Fixed.

Pointing at objects in main, with &, avoids new and delete. Deleting through a base pointer needs a virtual destructor, which is 14.01.
:::

<!-- Slide 45 -->

---

## Part 1: Check Your Work

- Each object prints its own line, including the base class object.
- The function is `virtual` in the base class.
- Each child's function matches the base's name, parameters, and `const` exactly.
- The array holds pointers to the base class, and the loop uses `->`.

::: notes
Walk the room. Every student should have a program that prints three different lines before starting Part 2; they will break that program on purpose.
:::

<!-- Slide 46 -->

---

## Part 1: One Possible Answer

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
~~~cpp
class Instrument {
public:
    virtual void play() const {
        cout << "An instrument makes a sound" << endl;
    }
};

class Guitar : public Instrument {
public:
    void play() const {
        cout << "Guitar strums: twang" << endl;
    }
};

class Drum : public Instrument {
public:
    void play() const {
        cout << "Drum beats: boom boom" << endl;
    }
};

int main() {
    Instrument horn;
    Guitar guitar;
    Drum drum;

    Instrument* band[3] = {&horn, &guitar, &drum};

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        band[i]->play();
    }
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::
:::

::: {.column width="40%" style="font-size: 60%;"}
. . .

~~~
An instrument makes a sound
Guitar strums: twang
Drum beats: boom boom
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
Show this after students have tried their own. Students without a working program use this one for Part 2.

Full program: cpp/activity_band_solution.cpp
:::

## Part 2: Break It

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}
Make one change at a time. Predict the result, compile and run, then put the change back before the next one.

| # | Change |
|:-:|---|
| 1 | Remove `virtual` from the base class function |
| 2 | Make the array hold objects instead of pointers, and call with `.` |
| 3 | Remove `const` from one child's function |
| 4 | Move `virtual` from the base class to one child's function |
| 5 | Remove `public` from one child's class line |
| 6 | Keep the pointer array, but call with `.` instead of `->` |
:::

::: notes
About 15 minutes. Have students write each prediction before running it: compile error, wrong output, or no change. The point is to connect a symptom to its cause, so the next time their own program prints the base class's line, they know where to look.

For change 2 with the solution code: Instrument band[3] = {horn, guitar, drum}; and band[i].play().

The answer sheet is assets/polymorphism_activity_instructor.md; each broken program is in cpp/activity_breaks/.
:::

<!-- Slide 48 -->

---

## Part 2: What Happened

::: {style="font-size: 65%;"}
| # | Change | Result | Why |
|:-:|---|---|---|
| 1 | No `virtual` | All three print the base line | Polymorphism is off; the pointer type picks the function |
| 2 | Array of objects | All three print the base line | Object slicing: each slot holds only the base part |
| 3 | Child loses `const` | That child prints the base line | A different signature is a new function, not an override |
| 4 | `virtual` only in a child | All three print the base line | `virtual` must be in the base class |
| 5 | No `public` | Compile error: `'Instrument' is an inaccessible base of 'Guitar'` | Private inheritance hides the is-a from `main` |
| 6 | `.` instead of `->` | Compile error: `request for member 'play' in 'band[i]', which is of pointer type` | `band[i]` is a pointer |
:::

::: notes
Ask students what changes 1, 2, and 4 have in common: three different mistakes, the same symptom. When a program prints the base class's version, check three things: is the base function virtual, is the call through a pointer or reference, and do the signatures match.

Change 3 compiles silently with g++ 11, even with -Wall -Wextra. clang warns that the child's play() hides the overloaded virtual function, and 14.01's override keyword turns this mistake into a compile error.
:::
